about: The words of the chain storm_vow (Data/encounters/chain_storm_vow_793.json; Design/content/chains/storm_vow.md): a vow made in a storm to Saint Cuthbert or to Thor, and the long way to keeping it. Every title, intention, line and label key of its fourteen cards; an outcome text for every option (keys '...out_<option>', named in each option's note: the engine shows the effects' own facts, the outcome texts are for the integrator); the four news items the cards post; one 'art.<card id>' line for each card's picture and one 'art.chain_storm_vow.ending.<name>' for each ending. Nobody is named in the words but saints, King Charles and 'the master' (Bede): the crew are the steersman, the lookout, the hand and the mate, and the forge or the spine names them. Nothing is quoted from a translation. What the abbot says of the letter follows Alcuin's letter of 793 to Wearmouth and Jarrow in our own words; what the lookout says of the rafts follows Bede's prose Life of Cuthbert c. 3 in ours; the wax riddle is Eusebius 31 and the storm riddle is the Exeter Book's, both given only as a line of our own and then as the game's own riddle items. People speak of days by feasts and seasons. Written 6 Oct 2026; a draft for the user to overwrite.

entries.text: The withy parts

Full dark and a full storm. The twisted withy that holds the steering oar to her side has parted, and she lies across the sea with two men hanging on the loom. Three of your crew are shouting, and only one of them is shouting about the oar.
The worst first. The withy has gone and she will not answer. There is a shore under our lee. I cannot see it. I can hear it.
Now what can be done. A rope on the oar and two men to it. And somebody with a free hand asks for help. Mine are busy.
Saint Cuthbert! He turned the wind for the brothers on the rafts when he was a boy, with the whole shore laughing at them. A candle as tall as yourself, and carry it to him. Say it!
The one who has the weather tonight is Thor. Promise him the best thing in the hold, and mean it. He has no use for wax.
And the best thing in the hold. Say that to the saint too. Saints can count.
Saint Martin holds one promise of yours already. Ask somebody who is not still waiting to be paid.
Vow Saint Cuthbert a candle your own height, carried to his island, and the best thing in the hold
Vow Thor the best thing in the hold
Promise nobody anything: get a rope on the oar

You shout it down the wind, all three parts, because the lookout shouts each one back at you until you do. The rope goes on the oar at the fourth try. Some time before light the noise under the lee is behind you, and nobody can say when that happened.

You say it once, loudly, to nobody you can see. The hand nods as a man nods at a fair price. The rope goes on the oar at the fourth try. Some time before light the noise under the lee is behind you. The lookout does not speak to you until noon.

You say nothing and go aft over the thwarts. The rope goes on the oar at the second try, and with three of you on the loom she comes round. Behind you the lookout and the hand are both still talking to the sky. You hear a little of what they promise it.

You say nothing and go aft. The loom comes across as the rope takes it and breaks two fingers of the man beside you. She comes round all the same. Behind you the lookout and the hand are both still talking to the sky, and what they are promising is yours.
What was said
The sea has gone down and the oar hangs on a new withy. Nobody has spoken of the night. Now the lookout does, because he cannot leave a thing alone, and the others stop what they are doing to listen.
I heard it and so did he. A candle of your own height. Carried to the island by you, not sent. And the best thing in the hold on the day you land. Three things. I counted them on the bailer.
The worst first. His island is the far end of England, and a candle that long eats two cakes of wax. Now the rest: wax is cheap where the Wends sell it, and nobody said which month.
You said the best thing in the hold. Not a good thing. The best. He took his time letting us go. I would not give him a reason to think again.
He has no house with a door. It is given where an ox is killed for him and men are watching. That is north. I know a man who will tell you the rest.

You said nothing, so I said it for you. A candle your height to Saint Cuthbert, carried by you, and the best of the hold. A boat's vow is the master's debt. That is in no book. It is true all the same.
I said a thing too. Mine was shorter. The best of the hold, to the thunderer. You may choose which of us lied to the sky.
Custom gives a vow a year and a day. I will keep a cord by the mast and put a knot in it each morning, so nobody need ask.
A man can say the wind made the words. I have sailed with two who did. One of them is still alive.
Stand by it: the candle, the journey and the best of the hold
Stand by it: the best thing in the hold, given in the north
Say you promised a gift, and a gift can be small
Say the wind made the words
You say all three parts again in daylight, which is harder. The lookout lets his breath go. The steersman cuts a length of cord, ties the first knot in it and hangs it by the mast.

You say it again in daylight: the best thing in the hold, in the north, before the year is out. The hand says, good. The steersman ties the first knot in a cord and hangs it by the mast without looking at either of you.

You say that a promise made with a mouth full of sea water may be read generously. Nobody argues. The steersman hangs his cord by the mast all the same, and the men go back to work a little too quickly.

You say the wind made the words and the wind may have them. The lookout goes forward and sits with his back to you. The steersman says only that the priest at Doccinga is a patient man, if it should ever come to that.
Heel to crown

The boat lies quiet. The lookout has borrowed a trough, a pot and somebody's fire, and stands you against the mast with a tarred line in his hand. He dipped the great candle for Easter when he was a boy, and has been waiting to be good at something aboard.
Heel to crown. Stand straight. No, as you stand when nobody is owed anything. There. You are a finger shorter than you think you are.
Two cakes of clean wax, a wick of twisted flax, and a week hanging before it will bear carrying. At home the cellarer weighed the wax out to us and weighed the stump back in.
The same line. I kept it. You have not grown, and the saint has not forgotten how tall you were.
There is a way with one cake: mutton fat at the heart and wax over it. It looks the same. It does not smell the same, and it weeps in the sun. I only tell you there is a way.
All that sea for what bees leave behind. Well. My people throw good swords into a lake. I say nothing.
An old abbot of ours made a riddle on it. The wax says: now I keep words, now I drive back the dark. Tablets and candles. I can say you the Latin while it sets.
Give him two cakes of clean wax from the hold
One cake, and mutton fat at the heart
Send ashore for wax at whatever is asked: a hundred and ten pennies
Not yet. Wax first, where it is cheap

He dips for two days, forty times down the trough and back, and will let nobody help. The candle hangs from the yard like a pale oar, your height to a finger. He says the old abbot's riddle over it in Latin, twice, the second time more slowly.

He does it and does it well, and does not speak while he works. The candle hangs from the yard, your height to a finger, and looks like any other. On the second warm day there is a bead of grease at its foot. He wipes it off before the others see.

The wax costs what wax costs when a man must have it. He dips for two days and will let nobody help. The candle hangs from the yard like a pale oar, your height to a finger, and he says an old abbot's riddle over it in Latin.

He coils the tarred line and puts it inside his shirt with his tablet. He says he will ask again. He does not say it as a threat, but the steersman ties the day's knot in the cord while you are both looking.
A hand's length

The candle lies along the thwarts in a wrapping of old sailcloth, and it has been seen. A woman in a good cloak gone thin at the hem has come down to the boat. She has stood there since the tide turned and does not mean to go.
My son has had a fever in his chest since the moon turned. The priest says a light before the altar, night and day. There is no wax in this place. The reeve had the last of it for the king's chapel.
A hundred and fifty pennies for that one. It is what I have. You can make another candle. I cannot make another son.
It is the saint's. It has been his since the night it was said. You would be selling what is not yours.
Then a piece. A hand's length off the foot. He will not miss a hand's length. Does he measure?
He has no need to. We did.
Cut her a hand's length from the foot, for nothing
Sell her the candle for a hundred and fifty pennies, and dip another
Keep it whole, and give her twelve pennies to send down the coast for wax
It is not yours to cut or to sell

You cut it with the ship's knife, a hand's length from the foot, and trim the wick out for her. She takes it in both hands like a living thing and goes without a word of thanks, which is the right way to go. The candle is now the height of a man who stoops a little.

She counts the pennies onto the thwart, some of them old and thin. Two of her people carry the candle up the strand between them. The lookout watches it go, takes the tarred line out of his shirt and says: two more cakes, then.

She looks at twelve pennies as at twelve days she may not have. Then she takes them, and asks which way the wax boats come. The steersman tells her, and tells her the name of an honest man there. The candle stays whole.

You tell her it is promised and that you may not cut a promise. She says she knows what a vow is; she made one herself this morning. She stands a while longer and then goes back up the strand. Nobody aboard speaks until she is out of sight.
Which of them
A slack afternoon with the sail asleep. The mate, who speaks perhaps ten times in a voyage, has been looking at you since noon the way a man looks at a knot he means to undo.
Which of them did you mean?
At home the priest stood us in the river and we said the words after him. That night my father went out to the tree as he always had. The barley came up.
Pay both. A candle to the one and a thing from the hold to the other. Then whichever of them it was has had his due.
And whichever it was not has watched you pay the other. I would sooner owe one lord than insult two.
I can say the whole of what they made us say. It is short. They wanted it remembered.
One debt, one creditor
Pay both: a candle to the saint and a thing from the hold to the thunderer
Ask him to say the words they made him say
You say a man who pays two lords for one night has two lords. The mate thinks about it for as long as it takes to coil a rope, and says that is also true. He does not speak again that day.

You say: both, then. The mate nods. The steersman crosses himself and looks at the water, and the hand, who has heard all of it, says the thunderer does not mind company; it is the other one who is jealous. The cord by the mast now counts for two.

He says them flat, in his own tongue, the way a man gives the marks of a channel: I forsake the devil, and all the devil's works and words, Thunaer and Woden and Saxnot. Then he says them again more slowly so that you have them. He does not say whether he meant them.
The pilgrims' sand
The island lies a mile off across wet sand that shines like a shield. The house's boatman stands at the edge of it with a pole taller than he is. He looks at the candle, and then at your shoes.
She is out for three hours yet. After that she comes round both ends at once and makes no noise about it.
Them that come to him walk it. Shoes off; the sand keeps shoes. At my heels, and off the grey patches. Or lie in the Ouse like a trader and carry it up from the boats. He gets his light either way.
Do not look for doors on the church. The heathen had them off for the hinges.
That is a hand short of you.
I know the way and the brothers know me. I could carry it over. But it was said: carried by you. I only say what was said.
Take off your shoes and carry it over the sand at his heels
Bring her round into the Ouse and carry it up from the landing
Let the lookout carry it over; see to the boat

The sand is colder than the sea. He walks ahead and does not look back, prodding with the pole, and you follow with the candle on your shoulder like an oar. Half way over he says, without turning, that most of them talk. On the far side a brother is waiting who has seen you coming for an hour.

You take her round with the flood and lie in the Ouse among the house's boats. The candle goes up the path from the landing on your shoulder. It is a shorter walk and a dry one, and the brother at the gate takes it from you as he would take a sack.

The lookout takes his shoes off before you have finished speaking. You watch him go over at the boatman's heels, small and then smaller, the candle a pale stroke on his shoulder. When you come round by the harbour it is already standing in the church, and the boatman does not greet you.
The tallest light in the church

The candle stands by the carved oak coffin at the right of the altar and is lit at the evening office. It is the tallest light in the church. When the brothers have gone out the bishop stays where he is, and asks what else was said in the storm.
It will burn to the Advent fast if the sacrist trims it. We have had few lamps since the heathen men came. He has had gold from kings, and I think he liked it less.
It will burn a season if the sacrist trims it. He has had gold from kings in his time, and I think he liked it less.
There is mutton fat at the heart of it. I have a nose. He has had worse from better men and taken it. But do not tell me it was all the wax you could find.
It is a hand short of you, and your lookout has told me who has the hand. Then it is whole. He would have cut it himself.
The boy carried it over the sand and you came round by the harbour. That is not how it was said. I only note it. I am not the one you promised.
Now the rest. The best thing in the hold. Men say that in storms and bring me a cheese.
If you ask me what is best in any hold, it is wine. Without wine there is no Mass, and we have said ours over the dregs since Lammas. But I did not make your vow.
There is the silk. I say nothing. I only know what is in the hold.
Lay the bolt of silk on the coffin: the best, as it was said and by the road it was said
Give two casks of Rhenish for the altar
Lay a hundred pennies on the altar in place of goods
The candle was the vow. Ask his blessing and go

You lay the bolt on the lid. The bishop looks at it a long time and says the saint was wrapped by poor men and will be wrapped again by rich ones, and this will serve. In the morning there are two books by your sea chest, in bare boards with the metal torn off, and silver from the saint's own rents; a strip of old linen, folded small, that came off the body when it was raised; an order for wine and wax at twice the price; and your house's name, he says, is in the book that is read at the altar.

Two casks go up from the landing on the brothers' shoulders, and the cellarer taps one before it is through the gate. The bishop says the saint drank water and his priests cannot. In the morning there is a book by your sea chest, in bare boards with the metal torn off, a little silver from the saint's rents, a strip of old linen that came off the body when it was raised, and an order for six casks more at twice the price.

A hundred pennies on a bare altar make a small heap. The bishop does not count them. He says silver is what a man gives when he would rather not choose, and that the house needs it and thanks you. In the morning there is a book by your sea chest, a strip of old linen that came off the body when it was raised, and an order for wine at twice the price.

He blesses you, the boat and the candle, in that order. He says that a man is the judge of his own words until he meets a better one. At the door a brother gives you what every pilgrim is given, a pinch of earth from the place where the washing water was poured, and the cellarer an order for wine and wax, because the house must buy from somebody.
No house with a door
The hand has brought an old shipmaster down to the boat: a man with a rope-burned palm and a stick, who looks into your hold before he looks at you, and takes his time over both.
He has been in more bad water than both of us and come out of it drier. Tell him what you said that night.
The thunderer keeps no house where you can leave a bundle. A thing is given where an ox is killed and men are sitting down to it, so that it is seen. Otherwise you have only dropped something.
At winter's start, when the beasts come off the hill. The hall above the market at Skiringssal does it, and the lord at Ogvaldsnes on the sound. Either. He is not particular about halls.
The Franks say we kill a man for a fair wind. A wind is not worth a man. An ox, a good blade, and he has been known to settle for drink.
Now. Best. Not dearest; any fool with a tally stick knows dearest. The best thing in a hold is the one your eye went to when the water came in. Which was it?
Say it was the sword, and let him put his mark on the scabbard
Say it was the wine
Say you will know it when you stand in the hall

He draws the sword a hand's breadth, breathes on it, and watches the breath go off the iron. Then he cuts three strokes in the scabbard with his own knife. Now it is spoken for, he says; sell it and you have sold another's goods. He tells the hand the marks of the way north, and you find you follow half of it.

He laughs once, like a block running. An honest man, he says: most say the sword and bring the wine. Take him two casks and let the lord's horn be filled first. They are dry up there before the feast and will pay well for whatever you do not give away.

He says that is a merchant's answer, and that the thunderer has heard merchants before. But he tells you the halls and the season all the same, and the hand walks him back up the strand with a hand under his elbow.
Winter's start

The beasts are down from the hill, an ox has been killed in the yard and the hall is full of the steam of it. The lord of the place has heard why a Frisian is at his door, and has had a bench cleared near the fire.
Sit. A man who crosses the sea to pay what he said in a storm can eat at my board. I know men who would not cross the yard.

It is done so. You say before these what you promised, and when. Then the drink goes round, his horn first. A blade goes into the tarn behind the hall, where he will find it and nobody else will. Silver the same. Drink, we drink.
The old man sent word which thing you named. I had it from a skipper before you were past the skerries. So did the thunderer, I expect.

Men sat at this board at midsummer who had been west over the sea, to an island with a church and nobody on it who could fight. They go again when the days lengthen. A river mouth this time, with two churches. I tell you because you are eating my ox.
Say it loudly. He is not deaf, but the hall is.
Say the vow before the hall, and give the marked sword to the tarn
Say the vow, and broach two casks of Rhenish for the hall, his horn first
Say the vow, and throw a hundred pennies' weight of silver into the tarn
Eat his ox, and say the thing is not aboard this voyage

You say it, and the hall is quiet for as long as it takes. Then you walk out behind the lord with half the benches after you and throw a Frankish sword into black water. It goes in point first and makes less noise than a fish. In the morning there are furs on your bench, marten and one bundle of sable, and four tusks; the lord says his door knows you now, and his own pilot will take you up inside the islands as far as you care to go.

You say it, the casks are broached, and the first horn is carried to the high seat and poured out on the hearthstones before any man drinks. After that it is a feast like another, and a long one. In the morning there are four bundles of marten and four tusks on your bench, and the lord says his door knows you now.

You say it, and walk out behind the lord, and throw a purse's weight of cut silver into black water in the dusk. The hand watches where it goes in, from habit. In the morning there are furs and tusks on your bench. The lord says silver is what a man gives who would rather not choose, but his door knows you now.

You eat, and when the horn comes round you say the thing you promised is not aboard this voyage. The lord says the thunderer has a long memory and he himself a middling one, and has your horn filled all the same. The hand does not sit with you. On the way down to the boat he says only: there is a priest in your steersman's marsh. Go and ask him, since you will not ask mine.
The cord is full
A year and a day have gone by since the night the withy parted. The men have counted; they keep a cord by the mast with a knot for every day, and today there is no cord left to knot.
The worst first. The year is out and the thing is not paid. The men look at the sky before they look at you.
Now what can be done. Swear it again before them with a nearer day, and go. Or ask a priest what a vow costs when it is not kept. The one at Doccinga will not shout.
With mine there is no priest to ask. There is only the next bad night.
You have sworn it twice already. I have no more cord.
Or say the wind made the words. I told you I had known two.
Swear it again before the crew: before this sailing season is out
Ask what an unkept vow costs: lay a course for Doccinga
The wind made the words. Cut the cord down

You say it again with your hand on the mast, and name the season. The steersman finds another length of cord, shorter than the first, and ties one knot in it. He holds it up so you can see how much is left.

You say you will hear what it costs before you decide whether to pay. The steersman says that is how his father bought cattle, and gives the course for the Lauwers mouth without being asked. The cord stays where it is.

You cut the cord down yourself and drop it over the side. It floats, which nobody expected, and follows the boat for a while. The steersman says the church on the mound at Doccinga is open to any man, even now. Nobody else says anything.
Another coin
The wooden church on its mound in the salt marsh, where the old bishop was killed. The priest is mending a sheep hurdle by the door. He hears the whole of it without putting the hurdle down.

A vow to a saint is a debt, and saints collect. I have buried men who found that out. But the books let a debt be paid in another coin when the first is out of reach: days on bread and water, or their worth to the poor, or a work.
You promised a devil the best of your hold. That promise does not bind. The making of it does, and the books have a price for that too. I did not write them.
You promised nothing. You let your men's promise stand in your hearing and then put it down. That is a smaller thing than breaking a vow, and a meaner one. The books have it.
You have been here before, and went away. The hurdle is the same hurdle. So is what I said.

Here is a work. On storm nights the boats cannot find this creek. We pulled two men out of the reeds last winter and did not pull out a third. A horn lantern on the mound from Martinmas to Easter, oil, and a boy to mind it: a hundred and fifty pennies sees three winters.
Or keep the fast. Forty days on bread, water and salt, and you bring the wax and the wine for the old bishop's day up this creek for no freight. The marsh will see you do it.
I was baptised in this house. I would like to be able to come back to it.
Pay for the light on the mound: a hundred and fifty pennies
Keep the forty days on bread, water and salt, and carry for the church for nothing
Pay for the light, and keep the fast as well
A vow to the wind is wind. Thank him and go

He counts the pennies on the church step and puts them in his shirt, and then at last puts the hurdle down. By evening the post is cut. The weavers of the mound send eight bolts down to the boat without a word about price: their men use that creek. The priest gives you the church's order for wine and wax, and says the lantern will be lit on Saint Martin's night whether you are here to see it or not.

Forty days is a long time to watch other men eat. You keep it, and carry the church's wax and wine up the creek on the day, and the marsh sees. The widow of the long mound, who feeds strangers before she asks their names, says she will keep whatever you leave with her and sell it when the price is right. Six bolts of cloth come down to the boat. The priest says the debt is paid, and that he would not make a habit of it.

You pay for the lantern and keep the fast as well, and carry for the church on the day with your belt drawn in. The marsh does not know what to make of a merchant who pays twice. It sends twelve bolts down to the boat, and the farmers of the long mound put two hundred pennies of their own toward the oil and give them to you to buy it with. The widow there will keep your goods. The priest says the saint is paid, and that he rather thinks the saint is surprised.
You thank him. He says you are welcome, and that the door has no lock, and picks up the next withy for the hurdle. The steersman stays in the church a while after you have gone down to the boat.
A new knot

The guest-master has a new knot in his cord of ships and has not ladled anything. A fisher of the house came in over the bar at first light: long ships lying under the island off the Coquet, a day's sail to the north. The abbot has come down to the mud himself.
Six, he says, or seven. He did not stay to count twice. Lying to, not fishing. Nobody lies to off the Coquet for pleasure.
We were written to last year. You live by the sea, the letter says, from which this plague first came. I have had it read to the brothers until they can say it. It does not say what to do.
You said you would come back and tell me if there were sails. You are here, and there are sails. I take that as it is meant.
They tell me you are a man who was heard in a storm. I do not ask you to be heard again. I ask what a man does who has a boat and a day.
The book chests. Father, the master's own books are in those chests. Plate can go in the ground. Books cannot go in the ground.
Up the river is all shoals above the island on the ebb. Go on this tide or not at all, and keep the south bank until the old wall.
Take the book chests up the river on this tide, and tell him to send for the reeve's men
Tell him: plate in the ground, boys inland, and the reeve's spears in the reeds by the bar
Kneel with the brothers, and sail on the tide

Nine chests come down to the mud on the brothers' backs and your cargo goes up the bank to make room. You take the flood up past the island with the lookout calling the south bank, and by dark the chests are under a thegn's roof inland with two brothers sitting on them. When you come down on the ebb there are spearmen in the reeds by the bar, and the abbot is having the altar plate buried under the calf pen.

Nine chests come down to the mud and you take the flood up past the island. Above it she touches, hangs, and lies over far enough for the river to come in across one chest before the men can shove her off; somebody's shoulder goes with the shoving. The chests reach a thegn's roof inland all the same, one of them dripping. When you come down on the ebb there are spearmen in the reeds by the bar.

You tell him what a man tells his own household: bury what will not spoil, send the boys and the old inland with the books on a cart, and have the reeve's men at the bar by night, in the reeds, not on the sand. He thanks you first, as he does, and then for once does not say no. A rider goes up the river bank before you have cast off.

You kneel with them in the stone church through one office, and it is a good one. Then the tide serves. The abbot blesses the boat from the bank. The lookout watches the two churches until the river bends, and after that he watches the sea to the north.
A roof on both

Broken ships lie on the south sand at the river mouth, ribs up, with gulls on them. The two stone churches stand on their rise as they stood, and there is a roof on both. The abbot walks you to the door and counts on his fingers what is still inside.

They came at first light, eleven days after you. They found the church swept, the chests gone and the reeve's men in the reeds by the bar. Their chief was killed on the mud. Then the wind got up from the north-east and did the rest.
Two days it blew. Them that came ashore alive did not get far.
The brothers say the saint sent the weather. I say it fell on both of us, and we were the ones standing on a hill. But somebody carried word, and that was not weather.
Every chest came back up the bank with its lock on. The master's own hand is in three of those books.
One chest took the river. Forty leaves have been drying on the refectory rafters like fish. They will read. I have looked at each of them myself.
The king has been told who it was. He is not a grateful man by nature, so I asked for you while he was still surprised.
The king who was told of it is dead, by his own men. His writing was made while he lived and the reeve at Eoforwic has seen the seal. I would use it soon.
Take what the house gives: two books, the reeve's silver and the cellarer's key
Take the house's gift, and the king's writing for the strand at Eoforwic
Ask only that the boat be named in the house's prayers on the master's day

Two books in plain boards, copied in this house: the abbot says they are what it has that travels. A bag from the king's reeve, who was glad of a fight he could win. And the cellarer, who likes merchants and counts it a fault, shows you the dry end of his store and says a bale left there will be there when you come back. The lookout says an English riddle over the wrecks on the way out, about who it is that stirs the sea from under.

Three books in plain boards, a bag from the reeve, the dry end of the cellarer's store, and a strip of sheepskin with a king's mark on it: this man's keel pays nothing on the strand at Eoforwic. The abbot says that a house which keeps the books of the dead should know what to do for the living, and that he is sorry it has taken a heathen fleet to teach him. The lookout says a riddle over the wrecks on the way out, about who stirs the sea from under.

The abbot thanks you first, and then says no: the boat will be named on the master's day for as long as the house stands, and you will take the books as well, because he has already had them carried down. The cellarer shows you the dry end of his store. The lookout stands in the door of the school a while, and comes back to the boat of his own will, saying a riddle about who stirs the sea.
The same sea
Hard weather again, and the same sea coming over the same quarter. This time nobody on the thwarts shouts a name at you. They bail. Now and then one of them looks aft, and then goes on bailing.
The worst first. It is as bad as the other night. Now the rest: the oar is sound, and nobody aboard owes anything.
His light is still burning, or the stump of it. The sacrist said to the Advent fast. I counted the weeks.
He has a thing in his tarn that he did not have before. I would not ask him twice in one life.
There is a light on the mound at home tonight, if the boy is awake. Somebody is finding the creek by it.
The brothers had a riddle on a leaf about who it is that stirs all this up from under. I will say it when I have a hand free.
Say nothing. Steer
Say thanks aloud for the last time, and promise nothing
Vow again

You steer. It blows itself out before morning, as they do. When there is light enough the lookout says his riddle, and the steersman takes the old cord with its year of knots down from the mast, coils it and puts it in your sea chest. He says a house should keep one thing that cost it something.

You say thanks aloud, to whom it concerns, and add that nothing more is offered. The hand laughs. It blows itself out before morning. The lookout says his riddle, and the steersman takes the old cord of knots down from the mast and puts it in your sea chest, where your heir will one day find it and wonder.

You begin to say it, and the steersman says over the wind, without turning his head: once is a debt, twice is a habit. You finish it anyway. It blows itself out before morning. The lookout says his riddle, and somebody cuts a new length of cord.
A Frisian skipper has brought a candle his own height to Saint Cuthbert's island for a vow made at sea. It burns by the coffin, the tallest light in the church.
A Frisian gave a Frankish sword to the water behind a lord's hall in the north, at winter's start, for a vow made in a storm. The lord has made him a guest of the house.
There is a lantern on the church mound at Doccinga on storm nights now, from Martinmas to Easter. A skipper who owed a saint paid for it.
This year the heathen men came to the monastery at the mouth of the Don and found it swept and watched. Their chief was killed there, and a storm broke their ships on the bar.

A small open boat lying across a breaking sea at night under torn cloud: the steering oar swinging loose at her quarter, the steersman and one man hanging on its loom, a thin boy standing at the mast with his mouth open to the wind, a grey-haired Northman bailing and looking up.

The same boat in a flat grey morning, sail drying: the boy counting three on his fingers with a wooden bailer in his other hand, the Northman whetting a knife, the steersman tying a first knot in a cord by the mast.

A boat on a strand at evening, a fire and a long wooden trough of melted wax beside her: the skipper standing against the mast while the boy holds a tarred line from his heel to his crown; a pale candle as long as an oar hanging from the lowered yard.

An English shingle strand at low tide, dull afternoon: a woman in a good worn cloak standing at the boat's side, a small leather purse held out; along the thwarts a man-long candle in old sailcloth, the boy's hand flat on it.

The boat becalmed, sail hanging, low sun: a big fair Saxon with a long knife across his belly sitting on a thwart with his elbows on his knees, looking steadily aft at the skipper; the steersman behind, looking at the water.

A mile of wet shining sand at the ebb with a low island beyond it: a short weathered boatman in a sealskin jerkin walking ahead with a tall pole, a barefoot man behind him carrying a pale candle on his shoulder like an oar, their prints filling with water.

Inside a plain timber church at dusk, the doorway open with no doors in it: a carved oak coffin raised by the altar, one great candle burning beside it taller than the gaunt white-haired bishop who stands with his hand on the lid; the skipper facing him.

A jetty at a northern market on a clear cold day: an old shipmaster leaning on a stick and looking down into the open hold of a small Frisian boat, the grey-haired Northman at his elbow, the skipper standing among his casks.

A long timber hall at night in autumn, a fire down the middle and a cauldron steaming: a lord in a blue tunic rising with a horn in his hand, benches of men turned to look at a Frisian skipper who stands holding a sword in its scabbard across both palms.

The mast of the boat close up, calm weather: a cord hanging from it knotted along its whole length to the very end, the steersman holding the last hand's breadth between finger and thumb, the crew looking at the sky.

A small wooden church on a green mound in a flat salt marsh under a wide sky: a sturdy priest with mud to the knee weaving a sheep hurdle by the door, listening, and the skipper with his hood in his hands; behind, a creek winding out to grey sea.

A tidal mudflat below two small stone churches on a rise, early light: a lean abbot with an ash staff, a round monk holding up a knotted cord, and a line of brothers carrying iron-bound chests down toward a beached boat.

A river mouth after a storm, torn sky clearing: the ribs of broken clinker ships in pale sand with gulls on them, a barelegged fisherman among them, and behind on the rise two stone churches whole, with smoke from a kitchen roof.

The boat in a gale at dusk, well reefed and holding her course: every man bailing or hauling with his head down, the skipper at the steering oar, and by the mast an old cord thick with knots swinging in the wind.
The great candle burned down to a stump in a pool of its own wax beside the oak coffin, a folded strip of old linen and a book in bare boards lying on a sea chest in the foreground.
A black tarn behind a hall at first light with one ring spreading on the water, and on the bank a pile of marten skins and four walrus tusks.
A horn lantern burning on a post on the church mound at night in driving rain, and far out on the dark water the small sail of a boat turning toward it.
A book chest standing open in a stone-walled room with coloured glass in the window, the books upright inside it, and through the door the wrecks on the sand.
